title: The Best Wines to Pair with Your Favorite Dim Sum Dishes
summary:
From beef rice rolls with Grignolino to veggie potstickers with dry Furmint, level up your dim sum feast.

The post The Best Wines to Pair with Your Favorite Dim Sum Dishes appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Dim sum translates, with poetic license to “touch the heart.” Indeed, a brunch-hour parade of Cantonese comfort snacks will make hearts young and old become “a flailing fawn,” the expression for hearts going pitter-patter in the dim sum heartland of Guangzhou. In the U.S., dumplings and buns tend to dominate, but they’re only part of the appeal; turnip cake, bone-in spareribs, and gelatinous chicken feet bring a range of textures and tastes that can further liven up the table.

Though tea is the typical pairing, wine has a way of enhancing the social aspect of dim sum while adding layers of flavor to the sprawling spread. If the restaurant allows, bring a few bottles to find your own mix-and-match favorites.

Har Gow (Shrimp)

The best har gow dumplings are stuffed with shrimp and only lightly seasoned to bring out the shrimp’s intrinsic sweetness. “Shellfish wines” like Muscadet, Albariño, and Chablis can work here, but try Carricante from Sicily. Its high acidity, notes of citrus zest and blossom, and a flinty or sea-spray minerality are a slam dunk with all kinds of seafood-based dim sum (like shrimp siu mai, scallop dumplings, and crab-filled soup dumplings).

Tornatore 2024 Carricante (Etna)

An herbaceous, floral nose unfurls aromas of lemongrass, pine needles, wild thyme and honeysuckle. The lemon expands on the palate, before the herbs and forest floor elements return to create a full, round sensation. 93 Points — Danielle Callegari

Inquire with the importer

Char Siu Bao (Pork)

These baked or steamed buns with BBQ pork in an unctuously sweet and savory sauce are often paired with pu-erh, a fermented and aged dark black tea. For wine, Mencía from Galicia is lighter and fresher than the more common Mencía from Bierzo, an intriguing combination of fine tannins, tart red fruit, and stony minerality on a lightweight, almost ethereal, frame. Like the char siu filling, it hints at sweet and savory with a touch of star anise. 

Alvaredos-Hobbs 2022 Mencía (Ribeira Sacra)

Inviting aromas of strawberry-rhubarb, dark chocolate and sagebrush open on the nose along with blackberry jam and hibiscus. The supple palate acknowledges svelte tannins that swoon on the finish like a boy band finishing their final ballad. Decant and drink now, or enjoy from 2027 onwards. Cellar Selection. 94 Points — Reggie Solomon

$40 Vine Republic

Potstickers (Vegetable)

Stuffed with greens, cabbage, mushrooms, and/or chives, crisp-bottomed veggie potstickers can be even more complex than their meaty counterparts, with underlying notes of ginger, garlic, and Shaoxing wine. All these pungent notes can be tricky to pair with wine, but dry Furmint brings its own complementary notes of citrus, ginger, smoke, and green chile, with light body and brisk, cleansing acidity. It has personality without obscuring the dumplings themselves.

Tempos Vega Sicilia 2021 Oremus Mandolás Dry Furmint (Tokaji)

White peach and cantaloupe flavors complement the tart lemon juice on the palate of this nuanced dry Furmint, which also has delicate floral and complex minerally notes. The finish is long and will have you reaching for another sip immediately if not sooner. 92 Points — Emily Saladino

$38 Wine.com

Rice Rolls (Beef)

A textural wonder, these slick, slurpy rolls are filled with chewy, richly seasoned beef; the two elements seem to call for opposing wines. Grignolino, a Piemontese grape with a growing presence in California, produces very light wines with surprisingly firm tannins. It can show flavors that play well with Chinese food: cherry, hibiscus, goji berry, roses, white pepper, and clove. It’s a good red option for all sorts of Cantonese dishes.

Braida di Giacomo Bologna 2023 Limonte (Grignolino d’Asti)

Grignolio, it is in the name, you cannot help but grin from this wine. Opening with aromas of drying raspberries, strawberries and cranberries that merge with notes of sage, thyme, and dusty earth on the joyful nose. Crunchy red berries pop on the palate, with blood orange and citrus notes adding a zestiness to the palate. The finish brings a savory twist of rosemary and mint, all elevated by vibrant acidity. A wine that also likes a chill. 93 Points — Jeff Porter

$28 K&L Wine Merchants

If you’re going with just one bottle, try a dry Alsatian Riesling. It has the body and ripe-fruit expression to pair with delicate cabbage or shrimp dumplings and sweet-and-smoky pork and beef preparations, and it harmonizes with salty, vinegary, and spicy condiments. And of course, Riesling’s trademark acidity cleanses the palate not just from fattier meats, but from the sheer quantity of food that is irresistible at a dim sum feast.

Domaine Paul Blanck 2019 Grand Cru Schlossberg Riesling Riesling (Alsace)

Full of flavor and confidently expressive, with guava and mangosteen lending an exotic edge to a core of yellow apple. The fruit is generous yet clearly defined, kept in check by bright, well-judged acidity that brings energy and structure. The finish is crunchy and precise, adding textural allure and extending the wine’s vibrant, layered character. Cellar Selection. 93 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$42 Saratoga Wine

title: NBA Champion Josh Hart Is the Winner of Our Wine & Culture Award
summary:
The avid collector and Knicks star is one of the most enthusiastic ambassadors for wine in sports today.

The post NBA Champion Josh Hart Is the Winner of Our Wine & Culture Award appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
For a few nights last June, it was normal to see groups of people—friends, complete strangers—crying tears of joy together in the streets of New York. First, it was over the Knicks’ miraculous 29-point comeback against the Spurs in Game 4 of the NBA Finals. Then it was when the team won the title for the first time in 53 years. For many New Yorkers, it was the biggest collective outpouring of happiness in their lives.

Josh Hart, the Knicks’ small forward and shooting guard, celebrated with a family trip to Bordeaux, where he stopped at the famed châteaux Mouton Rothschild, Latour, and Petrus, among others. At Château Lynch-Bages, he was treated to a six-bottle semi-blind test, which he aced. He also tried a 1995 Château Margaux, which he said was the best wine of the trip.

It was a dream vacation for Hart, who’s been serious about wine for the past six years and posts the exceptional wines he drinks on his Instagram page, Jhart Cellars. At a time when the wine industry is struggling to connect with large segments of the population, his passion is educating new audiences and bringing more drinkers into the fold. He’s one of the most enthusiastic wine ambassadors in sports today, and with his ambitions, what we see on social media is only the beginning. That’s why Wine Enthusiast is honoring him this year with a special Wine & Culture Award.

But Hart wasn’t always a wine lover. He grew up in Silver Springs, Maryland, in a family that never had wine at the table. His breakthrough came in December 2018, when he was playing for the Lakers. He bought a bottle of 2009 Harlan Estate for a secret Santa gift exchange with the team. They beat the Golden State Warriors on Christmas Day, and to celebrate after the game, they uncorked the Harlan on the team’s airplane. Even though Hart hated wine at the time, he took a sip. “I loved it,” he said. It was the first time he realized wine’s super powers.

“It was powerful but still elegant. It was also when we beat Golden State on Christmas. So, I think it was the notes of the wine, but also the memories and the experience,” he said. “That’s what got me into doing all this.”

Cut to 2026, and he’s a serious collector with a basement cellar stocked with bottles from the world’s most sought-after producers. While his collection is heavy on famous Burgundy and Bordeaux estates, he’s also been getting into Montefalco Sagrantino, specifically the wines of Paolo Bea. “He has probably four different wines, and I love them. It’s a really small region, very small production, and they’re amazing,” Hart said.

All told, he’s amassed over 1,000 bottles, and his collecting strategy has changed over the years. “I think for anybody in their wine journey at the beginning, you’re just buying everything, trying different varietals, different producers, seeing what you like,” he said. “And then as you start drinking more and more, you start to define your palate. So now I’ve gotten more into Amarone. Dal Forno Amarone is one of my favorite wines ever.”

When asked if there was a bottle that he’s never had but would love to try, he said Château Angélus. It was a delightful coincidence: When the Wine Enthusiast team went to his house to do the interview and shoot photos, we brought a 2023 Château Angélus as a gift, along with a 2023 Château Cheval Blanc. (Judging from his Instagram posts, we figured Bordeaux was a safe bet.)

Bucking the chillable, gluggable red trend, he’s also a fan of Rustenberg Wines’ Peter Barlow Cabernet Sauvignon from South Africa’s Stellenbosch region. “It was one of the best wines I had this summer,” he said. 

In August, Hart teamed up with the SuperVinoBros, media personalities known for their blind tastings, to shoot Instagram videos. Hart stumped them with the Peter Barlow. They returned the favor and blinded Hart on a red, and he guessed Cab Sauv from Napa. While it was actually Loire Valley Cabernet Franc, he was reassured it was a reasonable guess because the latter is the father grape variety of the former.

While Hart is clearly having fun these days as a collector and all-around wine guy, he has greater ambitions in the space. “I don’t know what my plans in the wine world are. I’m optimistic that I’m going to do something,” he said.

Three years ago, he launched a Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon called Bank Shot in collaboration with Maayan Koschitzky, but the long-term dream is a project that’s entirely his. “Obviously, I would love to come out with a wine of my own,” he said. “The huge goal would be to own some land in Napa. Seeing the prices now, though, that’s pretty tough.”

But in the immediate future, Hart is focused on his day job and winning another chip. Napa will be waiting for him.

title: South Africa’s Fine Wine Scene Has Grown Up with the Help of These Families
summary:
With centuries of family history, these Stellenbosch estates are like time machines.

The post South Africa’s Fine Wine Scene Has Grown Up with the Help of These Families appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
South Africa has been making wine for nearly four centuries. Yet the wine industry we know today is surprisingly young. How can both be true? For much of that history, winemaking was dominated by merchants and the cooperative system. Only in the last 50 years or so have estate bottlings and own-label wines given rise to a culture of fine wine.

The Love Story That Started It All

The country’s first crush took place in 1659. Another sort of crush blossomed not long afterward, between an enslaved woman and a German immigrant. Ansela van de Caab and Laurens Campher’s love story is intertwined with the genesis of the South African wine industry, helping create the mythology surrounding the historic Stellenbosch estate, Muratie.

In the early Cape, such relationships were not unusual; a European settler marrying an enslaved person, however, was virtually unheard of. Van de Caab (“of the Cape”) lived in a Dutch East India Company slave lodge and likely worked in the Company’s garden, where she is thought to have met Laurens, a soldier. They had three kids out of wedlock between 1686 and 1692. Laurens lived about 30 miles east of the Cape, in the Stellenbosch region, and would travel by foot or ox-drawn wagon to visit Ansela, who remained enslaved. After she was emancipated in 1695, Laurens brought her and the children to live with him at De Driesprong farm, which would later become the Muratie estate.

Visit Muratie today, and it’s like the clocks stopped in 1699, the year Laurens officially took over the property. The wooded farmyard is enclosed by whitewashed Cape Dutch buildings. Sprawling across the cellar entrance is an ancient oak tree that’s said to have been planted by Ansela to bless their marriage. Standing beneath this tree in the dappled shade, it’s easy to imagine Ansela and Laurens in conversation, as they are in the play inspired by their lives, Ansela van de Caab. In one scene, Laurens declares, “One day, I’ll come and fetch you. I want to marry you and have you always beside me, next to me, and you must be mine.”

Ansela replies, “How can I belong to you when I don’t even belong to myself?”

The Camphers planted 8,000 grapevines on the property and started making wine. The farm passed through a series of owners before Martin Melck bought it in 1763. It remained within the Melck-Beyers family for 134 years and was sold off again; in 1987, Ronnie Melck bought it back.

His son, Rijk Melck, the current owner, carries the soulful air of a poet. We meet in the tasting room beside the cellar, which is draped in thick cobwebs. Portraits of previous inhabitants hang on the crumbling stone walls, including nude studies of someone’s mistress, Amber. She, like Ansela, has a wine named after her; in fact, all the wines bear the names of characters from the farm’s past.

We head outside, and Rijk leads me to the original homestead, built by Laurens in 1685. Inside are thick, rough walls of clay, mud brick, and stone, crossed overhead by heavy timber beams. Rijk tells me that while the Campher bloodline is extensive, no one in the family is currently working in wine. Remarkably, though, his nephew married a direct descendant of Ansela and Laurens.

Muratie is one of the few Stellenbosch wineries that remains in family hands. “If you think about what’s around us, who’s left?” says Rijk, referring to the recent spate of historic estates being sold to foreign entities or divided up for property development.

Bringing Bordeaux to the Cape

Head south from Muratie toward the Eerste River, with the glittering Atlantic in the distance, and you’ll find another Stellenbosch family that’s still holding fast. Here lies South Africa’s oldest, and one of its most respected, family-owned estates. Meerlust, Dutch for “pleasure of the sea,” has been in the Myburgh dynasty since 1756.

At the end of the long, oak- and palm-lined drive, the white-gabled manor house glows gold through latticed windows. I arrive as they are throwing a party to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the first Meerlust-labeled wine, a 1975 Cabernet Sauvignon. The tinkle of glassware and laughter floats on the soft night air, as it has for eight generations of Myburgh family gatherings here.

The Meerlust farm was first established in 1693 and acquired by Johannes Albertus Myburgh in 1756. For the next six generations, the family sold wine in bulk, until a 1967 visit to France convinced Nico Myburgh that the estate’s maritime terroir was not dissimilar to Bordeaux’s. This revelation inspired Rubicon, a Bordeaux-style blend first made in 1980 with Italian winemaker Giorgio Dalla Cia. They named it for Julius Caesar’s river crossing, the “point of no return;” for them, it was a poignant coming of age. Released in 1980, Rubicon positioned the estate at the forefront of the country’s fine-wine movement.

Nico’s son, Hannes Myburgh, the current owner, is at the party. We’re in an old house, so naturally the topic of ghosts comes up. He hasn’t seen any himself but says a female specter has been spotted descending the staircase and rearranging the flowers in the vestibule. Hannes feels that the past generations are very alive here. “Children have chased one another through these rooms for centuries,” he says. “In a way, nothing changes. It stays the same.”

Hannes was, as he puts it, “promised to the land.” He says he had a carefree childhood, roaming the farm barefoot, catching fish in the dam. During school holidays, he was put in charge of irrigation in the vineyard. “It was damn hard work, but I loved it.”

After growing up in the family business, Hannes needed “free rein to become myself.” In 1976, he set out for Germany’s Rheingau region. Walking amongst vineyards that plunge toward the Rhine, something clicked: Suddenly he felt part of wine’s 8,000-year history.

He came home briefly in 1977 under sad circumstances: His mother was ill, and his parents were divorcing. The family stress prompted him to take a gap year in Paris, where he worked as a professional claqueur, someone planted in fashion-show audiences to start the applause. More consequential for his career was meeting members of the Rothschild family.

Hannes returned to Stellenbosch in 1982 and took over the vineyard, but went back to France the following year to work the harvest at Château Lafite Rothschild. This opportunity led to a watershed moment for both him and South African fine wine: He was invited to a dinner where Lafite 1961 was poured.

That bottle was his aha moment. “I experienced just how great wine could be,” he says.

His father died five years later, when Hannes was 31. “There I was, with the full responsibility of Meerlust,” he says.

Back at the party, in another room, someone drops a tray of wineglasses, snapping us back into the present. “Such a boring family, still living in the same old house!” Hannes jokes. “I’m 70 now, and having lived here all my life, this place is under my skin.”

Hannes has no children of his own. When asked the question of who takes over next, he smiles evasively. He reveals that there are some family members he is “really fond of.” In the cellar, succession has been rock-solid: Wim Truter is only the third winemaker since the first estate bottling in the 1970s. Hannes knows the wine is in safe hands.

‘You Can’t Make Good Wine in a Place That Looks Like a Hospital’

We move northeast now into the Simonsberg foothills, where Kanonkop, like Meerlust and Muratie, helped establish the modern Stellenbosch estate model half a century ago. Often compared to a Bordeaux First Growth, the winery has become a benchmark for age-worthy South African reds.

Kanonkop means “cannon hill,” and fittingly, a black cannon greets you at the top of the driveway. Centuries ago, the mountain peaks rang out with cannon booms to alert farmers that trading ships had entered Table Bay.

Unruly bushvines give way to old oaks on the approach to the cellar, which sits behind whitewashed walls. My visit coincides with the release of their 2023 Paul Sauer, arguably South Africa’s best Bordeaux-style red blend. After the tasting is a traditional snoek braai (fish barbecue), thrown by the estate’s owners, brothers Johann and Paul Krige, grandsons of former owner Paul Sauer.

Like many people who grow up on a vineyard, Johann once thought about leaving the family business. “Two years after I qualified as a lawyer, I realized I was too honest for the profession,” he tells me as he works the grill.

Kanonkop was once part of a larger farm called Uitkyk. In 1903, politician J.W. Sauer bought the property and lived there with his wife, Mary Cloete Sauer, and their children, including their only son, Paul. Mary, already of famous wine stock, was the daughter of Hendrik Cloete, owner of Groot Constantia, the Cape’s oldest wine estate, established in 1685.

After J.W. died in 1913, Mary remained at Uitkyk, where Paul began farming fruit and wine grapes; he also got into politics like his father. In 1929, Mary sold Uitkyk to a German nobleman, but excluded 85 hectares of undeveloped land from the sale. She gave this portion to Paul, who named it Kanonkop.

Paul is credited with saying, “You can’t make good wine in a place that looks like a hospital.” In other words, a cellar should have character. While he vastly improved the Kanonkop visitor experience, the vineyard still operated on the coop model and didn’t produce estate bottlings.

His daughter, Mary, inherited Kanonkop with her husband, Jannie Krige. In 1973, Jannie and winemaker Jan “Boland” Coetzee persuaded Paul to bottle a portion of the year’s yield under the Kanonkop name; a decade later, their son, Johann Krige, broke with co-ops entirely.

Kanonkop’s commitment to Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style wines made a strong case for Stellenbosch’s fine-wine potential. The estate has also championed Pinotage, proving to the world that the South African native grape can produce wines of complexity and ageability. Their Black Label Pinotage, made from a single block, is a sought-after, small-production wine with many devotees. Johann, in his typically unsentimental way, says, “One does not set about making a cult wine; it is a status bestowed upon you.”

Continuity in the cellar has been crucial: The reins passed from Coetzee to Beyers Truter to Abrie Beeslaar, whose two decades at the helm further cemented Kanonkop’s international reputation. Earlier this year, Dirk van Zyl was appointed head winemaker, bringing experience from the esteemed Glenelly Estate; he’s poised to make his mark.

“Nothing is promised,” says Johann of succession. “You have to work, prove yourself, be consistent.” Paul’s daughter, assistant winemaker Suzaan Krige, is doing just that. She is the first family member to ever join the Kanonkop winemaking team.

The fifth generation has arrived, and just in time. Urbanization is one of the greatest threats to South African wine, with housing developments eating away at prime viticultural land, taking pieces of these histories with them. Low grape prices, rising replanting costs, and the struggle to turn a profit are driving families to sell off their sprawling estates.

But with the likes of the Melcks, Myburghs, and Kriges championing both family and fine wine, you get the feeling the next act in this ongoing saga is a new beginning.

title: ‘White Wine Thrillers’ Are Trending. What Does Chardonnay Have to Do with Crime?
summary:
The new female-targeted genre proves that both entertainment and wine are still plagued by gender stereotypes.

The post ‘White Wine Thrillers’ Are Trending. What Does Chardonnay Have to Do with Crime? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
I recently had to defend my Cosmopolitan at a dive-adjacent Manhattan bar. 

“It’s a classic cocktail, actually,” I told my friend, who smirked while sipping a whiskey on the rocks. I blathered on about Carrie Bradshaw and the Cosmo’s historic significance as an emblem of New York City, admittedly striving to downplay its pink, fruity hallmarks and prove it qualifies as a “serious” drink, whatever that means. 

Perhaps linking a “girly” cocktail to a “girly” television show (albeit a prestige HBO hero series) wasn’t doing me any favors. But as new micro-labels hit the streaming era zeitgeist, the latest being the female-targeted “white wine thriller,” it’s evident that both entertainment and the beverage world are still plagued by limiting gender stereotypes.

The Era of ‘White Wine Thrillers’

In August, The Hollywood Reporter published a deep dive on the trending subgenre, linking the origin of the term “white wine thriller” to an unnamed Peacock executive, who used it during a conversation about female-led thrillers.

Anyone who has seen All Her Fault, Big Little Lies, or The Perfect Couple—the latter two series graced by Nicole Kidman in a wig—have experienced the mildly hair-raising buzz of a white wine thriller.

“A white wine thriller can get dark but not too dark,” wrote reporter Mikey O’Connell. “The body count is kept low. … There must be aspirational elements, typically wealthy characters wearing Brunello Cucinelli while emotionally unraveling in Nancy Meyers-worthy kitchens.” 

Often book adaptations that center female protagonists and target female audiences, these series are alluring and sexy yet fun and palatable … just like the stereotype of white wine. “White wine feels lighter, refreshing, enjoyable,” Lisa Katz, president of scripted content at NBC and Peacock, told THR. “It goes down easy.”

Its edgier sister, the “red wine thriller,” is as dark and complex as an aged Napa Cab. She leaves a gripping sensation in the mouth, a bleak feeling that sticks with you long after the credits roll. With more kills and more blood, “a red wine thriller stains your teeth, it’s tannic,” a producer told THR, which cited Sharp Objects and Hulu’s 2026 hit Furious as prime examples of red wine thrillers with mile-long finishes. 

The phrase “white wine thriller” is lighthearted and whimsical, but it’s hard to ignore the Chardonnay misogyny of it all. Entertainment centering women often acquires labels that are rarely given to media geared toward men. Think about it, what’s the male equivalent of a “chick flick?”

Beyond the world of entertainment, people have long wielded white wine as a rhetorical tool to minimize the significance and complexity of women, all while disparaging their taste. From satire articles depicting a request for ice cubes in a glass of “Chardy” as a womanhood milestone to Fox News deeming the middle-aged women who protest ICE “Chardonnay Antifa,” white wine-related nicknames for women are seldom kind, let alone accurate. 

The idea that all women prefer beverages and entertainment that lean light and refreshing over dark and complex is a notion that women wine professionals would like to dispel. Behind its playful veil, “white wine thriller” is just another infantilizing trope. 

White Wine and Stereotypes

Despite the gendered associations, the language we use to talk about red wine vs. white wine is often rooted in biochemical reality. 

“In general, white wine is meant to be consumed earlier and is overall less complex,” Rustic Canyon Family Wine Director Kathryn Coker tells Wine Enthusiast. “Red wine is generally more ‘serious’—they are considered more chemically and structurally complex than white wines because they ferment with the grape skins, seeds, and stems.”

Red wine is commonly described as bold, tannic, heavy, and spicy, while white wine is associated with crispness, lightness, and fruitiness. These are vital wine descriptors with true meaning, but other wine language perpetuates gendered stereotypes: A strong red equals masculine, while a sweet white equals feminine. 

“Whites have often been described in tasting notes using more feminine-coded language, while reds are described as ‘muscular’ or ‘masculine,’” says sommelier Michelle Chen. 

To Chen, the misconception that white wine is “easy, unserious, or entry-level,” perhaps a novice choice, is absurd.

“Some of the most complex, age-worthy, and collectible wines are white,” Chen says, calling Riesling a god-tier food-pairing option. “I think it teeters into misogyny when the type of wine a woman drinks becomes a proxy for her sophistication, emotional stability, or seriousness.” 

In Coker’s 15-plus years as a sommelier and wine bar owner, she can attest that women drinkers contain multitudes. A woman may enjoy a floral Riesling as deeply as a powerful red blend, and neither choice is indicative of her character or level of sophistication. “There is absolutely no ‘norm’ for women’s go-to in terms of wine,” she says. 

While Charlotte Marshall, sommelier and beverage director of Nic and Junior’s Tavern in Chicago, has observed women wine drinkers gravitating towards Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, she emphasizes that those happen to be “among the most approachable and widely available wines in the American market.” 

“Stereotypes have a place, and there’s data behind them, but staying too within them does a disservice to the guest and the wines,” Marshall continues. Indeed, there is some research to support the blanket statement that women prefer white wine, and it involves taste buds. 

Studies have shown that supertasting abilities appear in women more often than men. As for how that impacts wine preference, wine educator Dr. Liz Thach, MW, has noted that these “hyper-sensitive” tasters tend to avoid tannic and acidic wine, opting for whites and rosés. While research seems to indicate that many women gravitate toward white wine due to biological factors (a.k.a. superior fungiform papillae density), it hardly excuses any derogatory generalizations.

Natalie Dial, co-owner and wine director of Los Angeles’ Tomat, feels that the derogatory association between white wine or rosé and women is a distinctly American construct. 

“My guess is that the association between women and white wine is the modern-day equivalent of ‘suburban tranquilizers’ described by Betty Friedan in The Feminine Mystique,” Dial says. 

The 1963 book highlights the emptiness and discontent felt by many post-World War II American women, who were expected to find fulfillment in homemaking, modesty, motherhood, and marriage. Popping pill-form tranquilizers like Valium (a k a “Mother’s Little Helper”) and drinking alcohol offered an escape from domestic hell. 

“Once those prescriptions became more difficult to come by, of course we were reaching in the fridge for a cooling white wine to take the edge off of a long day jam-packed with patriarchy and repression,” Dial adds.

Chardonnay Girl Syndrome

Popular culture and entertainment certainly influence gender stereotypes in wine, and vice versa. “I think it’s a feedback loop between media and the cultural narratives that media then reinforces,” Chen says.

This interplay is painfully present in early-aughts film and literature. Renée Zellweger’s 32-year-old chain-smoking single gal Bridget Jones is the poster child for Chardonnay girl syndrome.

“I’ve failed again. I’ve poured an enormous glass of Chardonnay and I’m going to put my head in the oven,” reads one of her diary entries in the original 1996 novel, Bridget Jones’s Diary. The 2001 film adaptation of the same name is a complex piece of media when revisited; it was directed by a woman, Sharon Maguire, and the titular character herself is the exaggerated alter ego of her creator. Though endearingly pathetic and eternally relatable, a 136-pound, 30-something single woman who wishes to lose weight and “find a nice, sensible man” is a female character profile that has me needing something stronger than a glass of Chardonnay in 2026. 

The ABC (Anything But Chardonnay) movement of the mid-’90s spilled into the early-2000s, making it cool to turn one’s nose up at the buttery Napa Chardonnay that had oversaturated the market. By the time it became loveless Bridget Jones’ vice, the horn effect had already interfered and British sales sank.

“Chardonnay became associated with the single woman who is struggling and coping with her love life. Once that association was established, it became self-perpetuating,” Chen says of the romcom’s impact. This shallow association hasn’t entirely evaporated from mainstream culture, which is why terms like “white wine thriller” exude a similar level of sexism as “chick flick.”

To associate the seriousness of women to the seriousness of white wine, in this case Chardonnay, is already ridiculous, but it’s especially absurd given that some of the world’s most prestigious wines are Chardonnay-based.

“An oaky California Chardonnay might get stereotyped as ‘mom wine’ or saddled with more offensive terms like ‘cougar juice,’ while Grand Cru white Burgundy is treated as the domain of serious collectors, who are still culturally imagined as male,” she says. “In both cases, they’re drinking Chardonnay.”

The Horrors of Womanhood

The reality is, women are mocked no matter what they drink—Jones drowns her romantic sorrows in red wine, as well—or watch. Women are derided for being the predominant consumers of true crime, a gruesome genre that doesn’t exactly “go down easy.” If a woman can gulp a full-bodied Malbec while hitting “Next Episode” on a disturbing Netflix true-crime docuseries, then a white wine thriller can contradict the nickname it never asked for: they don’t always feel so fun and refreshing. 

Liz Meriwether’s red wine thriller Furious is a post-Epstein crime series that deals with sociopolitical issues like sex trafficking and domestic violence, with an overarching theme of female rage. Created by a woman, female-fronted, and undeniably feminist, the series’ red wine thriller label suggests its grisly elements somehow give it a masculine edge, as opposed to a “lighter” white wine thrillers like All Her Fault and Big Little Lies, both of which centralize the nuances of motherhood and female friendship. 

A heartwarming allyship between Sarah Snook and Dakota Fanning’s All Her Fault characters may soften the blow of a child kidnapping mommy witch hunt story, and Big Little Lies’ central murder is tonally alleviated by its ensemble cast of A-list Hollywood divas portraying the Monterey Five, a group of suburban wine-guzzling moms. A cardigan-wrapped Kidman gripping a glass of wine had become a TikTok meme, despite her character, Celeste Wright, being a battered wife. Vulture even released a BLL drinking game in 2017, leaning into the obvious wine mom coping phenomenon weaved into the show. “Mommy juice” and “rosé all day” vibes seem to cancel out what would otherwise be a tannic domestic violence plotline applicable to the red wine thriller label. 

Media depictions of women and wine are always evolving. Chen suggests Scandal’s powerful Washington D.C. “fixer” protagonist Olivia Pope and her oversized glasses of Shiraz have broadened associations between women and wine.

In the end, I will happily watch Queen of AMC Theatres Nicole Kidman in a wig on HBO alongside a bold Nebbiolo. Another night may call for a chilled glass of Pinot Grigio in my feminine little hand as Lola Petticrew (also in a wig) murders New York City’s most vile men. There are no rules.

title: No Hong Kong Trip Is Complete Without a Visit to This Hotel Bar
summary:
Newly ranked #25 on this year's 50 Best Bars list, Four Seasons Hong Kong's Argo looks to its home city for inspiration.

The post No Hong Kong Trip Is Complete Without a Visit to This Hotel Bar appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Hong Kong is the kind of intercultural, intertemporal urban hub that lends itself to creative world-building. Thanks, in part, to its history as a former British colony, the city is simultaneously Eastern and Western, and both ancient and futuristic—a combination its tourism industry leads with in its campaigns.

For decades, it’s been an artistic bellwether, with local auteurs and directors like Wong Kar-wai taking inspiration from the city’s past and reinventing it in films like Chungking Express and In the Mood for Love. Of course, the region’s cuisine also blends traditional roots with newer influences, but it really needs no introduction: if you’ve ever indulged in dim sum or char siu pork, you’re already familiar with the allure of Cantonese food.

Hong Kong’s bar scene is no different. Due to the region’s softer tourism policies (compared to mainland China), visitors have been flocking to the bustling archipelago for both business and pleasure for decades, so much so that Hong Kong developed a reputation as being a haven for “drunk-expats,” as we highlight in a story in our November 2025 print issue.

That has since changed, however, as both recent political upheaval in the region and the Covid-19 pandemic sent large numbers of expats packing. What’s remained is a reexamination of the city’s future, and a rededication to the heritage of Hong Kong, itself—in its drinks scene and beyond.

A shining example of this shift lies in the neighborhood of Central, just steps from Victoria Harbour, at the Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong’s flagship cocktail bar, Argo, and the world agrees—the bar ranked #25 on this year’s 50 Best Bars list.

The Decor

Walking into Argo feels like entering a conservatory set in the home of Jay Gatsby. Retro-style light fixtures hang from the ceiling, with terrariums and mirrors lining the walls that play with the abundant natural light streaming in through its massive windows (the Harbour view isn’t bad, either).

The balance between extravagance and warmth mirrors its Hong Kong backdrop. “When a guest walks into Argo for the first time, I want them to feel genuinely welcomed—not intimidated,” says Argo’s beverage manager, Jonathan Gabbay. “Hotel bars can sometimes come across as a bit too polished or exclusive. That’s never been the vibe we want.”

Argo’s pièce de résistance, however, is a towering, hauntingly beautiful bar structure, with backlit, shimmering shelves stocked with myriad spirits. It’s a mesmerizing centerpiece set in a perfect location—visible from the hotel lobby, the glimmering bar beckons to anyone who steps foot on the property.

The Drinks

Named for the ship Jason and his Argonauts helmed in their quest for the Golden Fleece, Argo and its menu seek to bring guests on a similar journey of discovery. Since he was named beverage manager in 2025, Gabbay’s mission has been to reshape the bar’s cocktail program into a “love letter to the city.” That mission now takes shape in Exploration—a new three-part menu that helped Argo achieve its #25 ranking on this year’s Best Bars list.

The menu’s first chapter, Local Encounters, looks to its home city for inspiration, crafting drinks in collaboration with local artisans, artists, and even a practitioner of Chinese medicine. A special shoutout goes to the Broth & Soul, a cocktail made in partnership with Big JJ Seafood Hotpot (a local spot with a cult following), which combines Grey Goose vodka, clarified tomato juice, and sherry infused with hotpot spices.

The next section is Seasonal Journeys, which, true to its name, shifts its focus to the seasonality and terroir of the region. Here, classic cocktails spotlight local ingredients, resulting in concoctions like the Floral Martini, which uses a tincture made from local flowers, and a Fruity Highball that combines Glenlivet 12 Y.O. with a fruit cordial and tea.

Finally, Exploration concludes with Timeless Passages, a selection of ten Argo favorites that have been captivating guests since the bar opened in 2021. The flagship Argo Martini employs the bar’s own Argo Gin, crafted with help from South Australia’s The Never Never Distilling Co.

The Crowd

Given its critical acclaim, as well as its Four Seasons Hong Kong setting (whose culinary and bar team currently maintain seven Michelin stars across the hotel’s Lung King Heen, Caprice, and Noi restaurants), expect to see both curious and in-the-know guests from all over the world. “Argo is for everyone. Every kind of drinker,” Gabbay says. “It’s a safe place and a sharing place. You don’t need to know the industry or speak the language of cocktail bars to belong here.”

Argo is open to the public, and accepts both walk-ins and reservations. For a more personalized experience, guests can also enjoy Argo’s Exploration menu in its private, botany-inspired Glass Room.

The Bottom Line

In Hong Kong, great cocktail options abound. And while the city is currently home to four of the world’s top 50 bars, according to 50 Best—including the #1 spot, Bar Leone—Argo’s dazzling interior and its commitment to Hong Kong craftsmanship make it stand out in a town full of standouts.

If you’re planning a trip to the region, make sure to check out our guide to Hong Kong’s electric bar scene, and don’t forget a stop at the Cathay Pacific lounges at Hong Kong International Airport—a wonderful drinks experience in itself, with bartenders whipping up classic cocktails, as well as the airline’s signature Cathay Delight mocktail, a blend of kiwi juice, whole milk, coconut milk, and mint leaves.

title: We Cracked the Code on a Low-ABV Margarita
summary:
Agave wine stars alongside lime juice, agave syrup, and orange juice in this low-alcohol spin on the classic margarita.

The post We Cracked the Code on a Low-ABV Margarita appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In one of the most popular cocktails at Mediterranean restaurant Sipeos, which serves only beer, wine, and zero-proof cocktails, low-alcohol agave wine stands in for traditional tequila. “It’s balanced and you still taste the agave,” Piccione assures. “If you didn’t know it was low abv, you wouldn’t be able to tell.”

Agave wine, a sap extracted from blue agave that’s fermented with yeast and fortified with a small amount of an agave spirit, is growing increasingly popular in the United States. In this lower-abv margarita, the agave flavor “really shines through,” says Piccione.

Low-ABV Margarita Recipe

Courtesy of Vincenzo Piccione, bar manager, Sipeos, Walnut Creek, CA

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Ola Sol agave wine
  • 1 ounce lime juice
  • ½ ounce agave syrup
  • ¼ ounce orange juice
  • Lime wedge, for garnish

Directions

Step 1
Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice.
Step 2
Shake well.
Step 3
Strain into rocks glass over fresh ice. Garnish with lime wedge.

title: Vintage Menus Are a Glimpse into the Golden Age of Dining
summary:
Eugen Beer and Barbara McMahon aim to preserve dining culture through their enormous collection of vintage menus.

The post Vintage Menus Are a Glimpse into the Golden Age of Dining appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In 2012, Eugen Beer, a British publicist, and Barbara McMahon, a Scottish journalist, were working on a project at home in the U.K. While searching through the University of Nevada’s online archives, they came across an old menu from Café Anglais in Paris, which closed in 1913. It featured a little boy feeding a piece of meat to the moon

“We were just completely charmed,” Beer says. “It opened a giant rabbit hole for us.”

The couple became engrossed in a world of menu collectors, archivists, and dealers they never knew existed. More than a decade later, they’ve pored over thousands of menus pulled from cardboard boxes and library shelves across the U.S.

They’ve found hand-painted cards from late-19th-century New York banquets, keepsakes from the golden age of cruise liners, and mid-century masterpieces made for Hawaiian hotels. They’ve unearthed forgotten commercial work by Saul Bass and Paul Rand, two of the 20th century’s most influential graphic designers. They even found a menu from 1947 that William Steig—the creator of Shrek—designed for Welton’s in Worcester, Massachusetts, listing Cognac at 75 cents.

Today, Beer and McMahon run the business Vintage Menu Art, selling menu prints from their ever-growing, 1,500-strong catalog. But if you ask Beer, the commercial appeal is almost beside the point. It’s more about their passion for preserving dining culture. “It’s a slice of Americana that Americans forgot,” he says.

Dining at restaurants became a part of American life just before the turn of the 20th century. As manifest destiny led Americans westward, cities sprang up across the heartland, creating new demand for hotels, restaurants, and bars.

“There was no dining-out culture in the U.K.—except for the very rich—until the ’60s,” Beer explains. “But in the U.S., whenever a place like Dodge City emerged, one of the first things they did was establish a hotel and import a bartender from the East Coast.”

Then, after Prohibition, restaurants boomed nationwide, and their owners began commissioning artists to make their menus stand out in an increasingly crowded field.

“The food at that time was all the same. It was steak, it was lobster, it was burgers,” Beer says. Whether it was promoting the zombie cocktail in Waikiki or the art of enjoying wine, the menus were a colorful form of marketing that helped turn ordinary meals into nights to remember.

In retrospect, they also reveal how restaurants kept drinks cheap to compete with other spots.

“Immediately after Prohibition, in 99% of places, cocktails would have started at 25 cents,” Beer says. “We have one menu from Tail o’ the Cock in the 1940s. The most expensive dish, a filet mignon, was $4.95, and a bottle of Château Margaux was $5.75.”

The U.S. was fertile ground for menu hunting for another reason: Americans held onto them. For generations, people kept menus tucked into scrapbooks, a practice Beer attributes to both rising purchasing power and a distinctly American appetite for souvenirs.

The golden age of menu design flew under the radar for decades, but some of them eventually found their way into private and institutional collections. By the early 2010s, the Culinary Institute of America in New York alone had up to nearly 50,000 menus. Getting access to them was surprisingly difficult, though.

“At the New York Public Library, you’d have to book an appointment. You could only see two menus at a time,” Beer says.

Private collectors offered another way in. One was Henry Voigt, a former DuPont executive who started buying menus at auctions in the 1990s and eventually amassed more than 10,000. Beer considers him one of the foremost custodians of American menu art, and he agreed to let the couple work with his collection.

Ever since, Voigt has been a key inspiration and resource for Vintage Menu Art, which sells prints from his collection. Voigt has also donated more than 2,600 pre-20th-century menus to the American Antiquarian Society. Voigt would say he’s simply preserving “the history of everyday life.”

“[These menus] not only reflect what the people were eating but also what they were doing and what they valued—the symbolism of food,” Voigt tells me.

He says a menu can transport you to a moment in history, like one in his collection from Springfield, Massachusetts, dated April 16, 1865, the day after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination. Its black border looked like a printing error at first. Then Voigt realized it was printed that way to mourn the president’s death.

“You put yourself in that dining room,” he says, “and through dinner, you’re hearing church bells all over Springfield because they rang all day that Sunday.”

For Beer and McMahon, rescuing forgotten menus is a labor of love. First, they scour auctions and follow leads for unique pieces. “We don’t care if it comes from Poughkeepsie or Punxsutawney. Does the menu speak to us?” Beer says of their search criteria.

Those that make the cut are scanned and cleaned up, pixel by pixel, removing creases, stains, and other damage. They also research the stories behind the designs, packing as much history as they can into each reproduction, including original menus, prices, and all. Then, they print them on archival paper and sell them online, at their permanent booth in L.A.’s Farmers Market, and at art and wine fairs on the West Coast.

Now, between museums and commercial print sales, these menus are reaching new audiences again. Beer says they still achieve what their creators intended.

“These were designed to entertain, to make people anticipate a nice time, and they’re still doing that,” he says. “When people pick up a print [at our stall in L.A.], they go, ‘Wow, have you seen this?’ They whip themselves up into a frenzy of excitement.”

title: These Italian Wine Family Dynasties Have Been Reigning for Centuries
summary:
Through centuries of upheaval in the Italian wine world, these five families have endured and become icons of perseverance.

The post These Italian Wine Family Dynasties Have Been Reigning for Centuries appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Hold tight to tradition, study the past, respect your elders: These are the rules in Italy. Legacies are meant to be maintained, and ostensibly nowhere does this matter more than in the wine business.

But a deep history can also be a mirage. Take, for example, the so-called “Carbonaragate” scandal. A decade ago, a French website published a bad carbonara recipe video. In lieu of the traditional preparation—pork cheek and pecorino quickly tossed with tempered egg yolk over spaghetti or bucatini—it used onion, bacon, bowtie pasta, and crème fraîche, boiled together in a pot, then topped with a raw egg.

A rage-fueled media frenzy started in Italy and spread around the world. It was more than just a miserable execution of a classic Roman pasta dish; what Italians really couldn’t forgive was the audacity of someone assaulting the timehonored, immutable foundations of their cuisine.

The irony is that carbonara has only been around since maybe the end of World War II. Though the idea of Italian identity dates back to the Roman Empire, Italy didn’t exist as a unified country until 1861 and didn’t start exporting a singular “Italian” cuisine until around 75 years ago. Most of the Italian food staples the world knows are relatively new.

There are a few exceptions, like the holy trinity of bread, olive oil, and wine. Wine has been produced on the peninsula for thousands of years, perhaps longer. That said, the Italian wine we drink today is, in many ways, very young—the vines, the land, and the people who work them have changed so much over the past few decades.

After the creation of the European Economic Community in 1957, open trade across the continent encouraged regions with extended growing seasons and fertile terrain—especially Italy, particularly in the south—to shoot for quantity over quality. Wineries then sold their grape must to less blessed agricultural areas, where achieving phenolic maturity and a high alcohol content were constant challenges. Super juice from southern Italy was used to pump up their final product.

In 1964, the sharecropping system that had sustained most of Italy’s agrarian estates for centuries started to dissolve. This led many multi-generation winemaking families to sell their land or convert it to other purposes. By the 1970s, Italy was still producing far too much grape must, so the government incentivized families to destroy their vineyards, and many thousands of hectares of old vines were ripped out.

All this means that, much like carbonara, most Italian vineyards can’t claim to be continuous commercial estates that predate the mid-20th century. Many celebrated Italian winemaking families today have made wine for themselves or their immediate community for generations, some going back to the Middle Ages. But very few have been operating professionally that entire time, making the same wine, from the same land, with the same people, for more than a few decades. Here are five iconic Italian wine families that have stood tall while withstanding these transformations and challenges—and are now absolutely towering.

Pio Cesare

When Cesare Pio founded his winery in 1881, the nation of Italy was still in its infancy. Pio’s passport was one of the first issued by the new country—number 55—and remains in the family’s archives. He can be credited with setting the foundation for a future that would ultimately see the wines of Piedmont become some of the most celebrated in the entire world.

In the 19th century, Cesare Pio identified the unique terrain in the Langhe that could maximize the potential of their native grape and bring to life an exceptional Piedmontese wine. But Nebbiolo, finicky in the vineyard and austere in the bottle, was not necessarily suited to changing trends. At Pio Cesare, attention has been given to shaping Barolos and Barbarescos that carry the weight of their history while offering increasingly accessible elegance.

Managing Director Federica Boffa, who is in the fifth generation of the Pio-Boffa family, knows she has her work cut out for her. “We understand that it is a BIG [emphasis hers] responsibility connected not only to our family but also to our city, our region, our appellation, and our terroir,” she says. “Climate is definitely not helping us in making this task easier, not guaranteeing we will still be able to grow Nebbiolo in the future with the same authentic expression of the past.”

She also knows that the more people drink these wines today, the more likely she is to guarantee Pio Cesare’s success tomorrow. “Barolo and Barbaresco are very democratic wines, not to be presented only in a jacket and tie, but also in jeans and a T-shirt,” she says. To do this, Boffa tries to employ a more informal approach in all senses: using simpler language, pairing the wine with many different cuisines, and presenting it not only in formal dining venues but also in relaxed bars and cafés. She insists that history shouldn’t make Barolo feel challenging, but should instead add to its appeal, making it more “cool, fun to enjoy,” not less.

Boffa’s democratic approach to wine reflects changes in social politics that extend far beyond the cellar. If at one time making Barolo feel exclusive and elite was a means of lifting it out of obscurity, now an inclusive, expansive approach will allow it to spread its wings.

Pio Cesare 2022 Bricco di Treiso “Il Bricco” Nebbiolo (Barbaresco)

From the highest plots of Bricco di Treiso, Il Bricco has carried the clear voice of this vineyard since 1974, and a difficult vintage has done nothing to quiet it. Warmed cherry compote, crushed strawberries and dried herbs finely worked together offer a savory, uplifting complexity. The palate answers with generous baked plum and raspberry, tannins open and welcoming now but very much built to travel. Drink now to 2040. Cellar Selection. 95 Points — Jeff Porter

Inquire with the winery

Tenuta San Leonardo

San Leonardo is a storied estate in northeast Italy’s Trentino region. Reflecting on the moment he took over, Marchese Anselmo Guerrieri Gonzaga recalls, “When my father passed me the responsibility for San Leonardo, he asked me to ‘take care of it.’” Simple words, but deadly serious ones if you’re about to take the reins of vineyards that have been in your family for 300 years.

Indeed, there was no question what his father meant by taking care of this place—keeping things the way they had always been. “One lesson I was taught was to remain completely faithful to the past and to be very conservative about change,” Guerrieri Gonzaga says.

But being a custodian of your family’s legacy often means finding solutions to future threats. While San Leonardo was known for just one wine—a spectacular Cabernet Franc-forward blend often ranked among the world’s greatest—Guerrieri Gonzaga intuited a need to meet the moment, and that meant new grape varieties.

“I felt we needed to bring San Leonardo to a wider audience and show that we could create wines for different occasions,” he says. “This gave the estate new energy and allowed more people to discover our work, while keeping San Leonardo at the center of everything.”

The introduction of a cru Carménère and white wines has changed their production substantially, but their practice stays the same. The new wines have also allowed the San Leonardo team to show the breadth of their talents.

Paraphrasing the famous lines from the Sicilian aristocrat Giuseppe Tomaso di Lampedusa—who observed that in order for everything to stay the same, everything must change— Guerrieri Gonzaga says, “I wanted to preserve what my father created, while allowing the estate to grow. Perhaps what I discarded was the idea that being faithful to the past means keeping everything exactly as it was.”

Tenuta San Leonardo 2024 Vette Sauvignon Blanc (Vigneti delle Dolomiti)

Like hiking through an alpine meadow with a basket of citrus. The freshness hits different here, more crystalline than crisp. This is the wine equivalent of that perfect summer day when everything just feels right. Grilled shrimp would make it even better. 91 Points — J.P.

$23 Liquor Pantry

Marchesi Antinori

In the Italian wine world, there may be quibbles over the length of a family’s legacy, but one name ends all arguments. Giovanni di Piero Antinori joined the guild of winemakers in Florence in 1385, and his successors have made wine ever since in their home territory of Tuscany.

Many of their iconic bottles have both created and then transcended the trends that have defined global wine-consumption patterns. From its beating heart in Chianti Classico, the Antinori family network stretches out to Montalcino and Bolgheri, and then well beyond to Puglia, Piedmont, and Franciacorta. Recent years have only seen their presence explode further in the U.S., with the acquisition of Napa Valley’s Stag’s Leap and Washington’s Col Solare.

To say that Marchese Piero Antinori has a lot of history to carry is an understatement. He has learned to be agile in both diversifying holdings and facilitating the passage of so much responsibility. His daughter, Albiera, is now the president of the company, with her sisters Allegra and Alessia serving as vice presidents. In his current role as honorary president, Piero can now appreciate that change is inevitable, often to the benefit of legacy. “In the 24 generations that preceded me, the rule was that only sons should run the business,” Piero says. “In my case, for the first time, I did not follow this rule. Having only daughters, I had no choice. I am glad to say that, considering the results, I consider this change a positive development.”

Marchesi Antinori 2021 Buiano Castellina Gran Selezione Sangiovese (Chianti Classico)

The nose is earthy and floral, with aromas of top soil, tulips and cherries, plus a bit of chocolate for nuance. The palate brings an intensity and layering of flavors that makes you sit up and pay attention, as an umami earthiness emerges first, then high notes of sweet cherries, and finally a finish where that hint of chocolate from the nose takes over. 96 Points — Danielle Callegari

$145 Zachys

Emidio Pepe

Emidio Pepe bottles have become cult objects because they are pure expressions of the earth. They became sought-after wines following the 1960s, when Emidio Pepe first took steps to engage with sustainable, regenerative farming and low-intervention winemaking, becoming part of a revolution that later metamorphosed into the natural wine movement of today.

But the Pepe family should be given its due when it comes to longevity debates. They’ve made wine without interruption on this land since 1889, when it was called Casa Pepe. That’s no small feat anywhere on the peninsula, and even more impressive in Abruzzo, long dominated by co-operatives and still dogged today by a reputation for making more grape juice than great labels.

Emidio Pepe passed away this summer after 94 magnificent years of living and breathing wine, but his work continues in the capable hands of his granddaughter, Chiara De Iulis Pepe. Yet to arrive at the age Dante called the midpoint of our lives (35), Chiara is already an internationally acclaimed winemaker steering the Pepe ship with a vision that’s making waves well beyond the Adriatic. “I have to keep doing things that are a little bit weird, a little bizarre,” she says, “because that’s what defines this place.”

While change and growth are her constants, she perceives tradition as antithetical to stagnation. “[Tradition] is not something you carry like a backpack or a heavy burden,” she says, “it’s something that you’re a part of. You have to see tradition through a dynamic lens, in which things are moving.”

Her grandfather planted pillars for her, as she describes it, but there’s plenty of room for her to dance in the space between them. That freedom to move keeps her limber enough to hold those pillars high.

Emidio Pepe 2022 Montepulciano (Abruzzo)

A very umami, savory nose of pepper, earth, hot tar, crushed rocks and old leather is balanced out by a palate that presents tart berries and lots of citrus, beneath a sprinkle of salt and pepper. The finish unveils a spiced, bitter cocoa element, wrapping up a wine which is layered, dense and substantial, but also agile, directed and linear. 95 Points — D.C.

$150 K&L Wine Merchants

Tasca d’Almerita

Wineries in southern Italy were the most likely to be uprooted by the 20th century’s seismic upheavals. So the fact that the Tasca family’s flagship estate, Tenuta Regaleali, remains firmly grounded on 550 hectares in the middle of Sicily is nothing short of a miracle.

Even more surprising, the property hasn’t changed hands, or much else, since 1830. The vineyards are still dedicated to a mixture of native Sicilian grapes and international varietals, crafted into wines that seem earthquake-proof—safely attached to their foundation, but with built-in flexibility that allows them to bend in a new direction without breaking. The eighth generation is now preparing to take over the estate, along with four other properties that have been added to their roster over the years, allowing them to vastly expand their global reach.

If Alessandro Tasca is nervous about the shoes he has to fill, he mostly takes it in stride. “What scares me most is probably also one of the best parts of the job: working with my family,” says Alessandro, who is preparing for a leadership role in the future. “Being part of a family business is special because you are building something together with the people closest to you. At the same time, that is exactly what can make it difficult. Business relationships and family relationships do not always remain separate, and disagreements at work can easily become personal.”

With a lot of cooks in the kitchen, things can get hot quickly. Tasca takes the long view and decentralizes himself to get perspective: “My role is not simply to inherit what previous generations built, but to protect it, improve it, and eventually pass it on to the next generation. Thinking this way helps me remember that the legacy is bigger than any one person.”

Tasca d’Almerita 2020 Tenuta Regaleali Nozze d’Oro White Blend (Sicilia)

Melon, pear, apple and a hint of white peach are on the nose. The palate is juicy with more pear and melon, with the sweet, slight astringency of candied lemon peel and a welcome salty note, like licking a rock. 92 Points — D.C.

title: The Best Mezcals of 2026 to Gift (or Keep for Yourself)
summary:
WE Writer-at-Large Kara Newman shares the year’s best mezcals to sip or stir into cocktails—including one with a perfect 100-point score.

The post The Best Mezcals of 2026 to Gift (or Keep for Yourself) appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In an age where mezcal bars are plentiful and the Mezcal Old Fashioned is considered a modern classic, it’s hard to believe that just a few years ago, few Americans knew about this Mexican liquor distilled from agave. 

Today, mezcal is firmly in the mainstream, and as popular as its cousin tequila, also made from agave. They belong to one of the few spirits categories that continues to see growth. According to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, tequila and mezcal sales totaled $6.4 billion in 2025, which places the category right behind vodka, the longtime market leader.

A key reason for its continued popularity: mezcal offers plenty of discovery opportunities for curious agave fans. Compared to tequila, made with a single cultivar of agave (Blue Weber) within one of five regions in Mexico, mezcal can be made from more than 20 agave species—Espadin is the best-known—within nine Mexican states. No wonder mezcal offers such a diverse array of expressions, from citrusy and crisp to smoky and savory. And to clear up an oft-cited stereotype: No, not all mezcals are smoky.

Furthermore, not all mezcals are clearly labeled as “mezcal.” For a spirit to be officially certified as such, producers must pay a fee, and many of them opt to skip the cost. Instead, their products are classified as Destilados de Agave (literally “distillates of agave,” or “agave spirits”).

Many of those spirits are excellent: a destilado de agave by Cazcanes, a Jalisco-based producer of small-batch spirits, earned a perfect 100-point score from one of our critics. The Cazcanes Destilado de Agave Nuestras Raices Still Strength Blanco is a wild and expressive spirit that unfolded bell pepper, jalapeño, lime peel, and crumbled sage, plus a surprising hint of cacao.

In the years to come, mezcal will most likely continue to command attention. Consumers—particularly younger audiences—are increasingly choosing drinks that are authentic, bear a sense of place, and tell a story, and a lot of mezcal fits the bill. Here are a few of our favorite mezcals of 2026.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

El Silencio Mezcal Rare

This complex mezcal unfolds salinity and tropical funk, resulting in sea breeze-y, aged cheese-y, and lightly fruity flavors. Ripe banana, lychee, rosewater, and a hint of almond sweetness linger into a lip-smacking finish dotted with pink peppercorn and sea salt. Made with espadin and bicuishe y barril agaves. 97 Points — K.N.

$187 Lost N Liquor

Rosaluna Mezcal

Made with single estate-grown espadin agave, this mezcal has a bold dried oregano scent. The palate shows jalapeno, graphite, and dried herbs, finishing with a sooty exhale and black pepper heat. 93 Points — K.N.

$32 Total Wine

Dady’O Mezcal

This espadin has a lightly smoky scent. On the palate, that campfire smoke quality mixes with tinges of dark chocolate and sea salt, plus a roasty, warming finish. Best Buy. 93 Points — K.N.

$50 Keg N Bottle

Los Perdidos De La Noche Tepeztate Mezcal Reposado

Four months of aging in casks that previously held Cognac lend a pale straw hue to this mezcal, made with tepeztate agave. The first sips lead with jalapeno and graphite, softening into banana tinged with vanilla. The drying exhale is warmed with a flurry of black pepper plus a hint of anise. 92 Points — K.N.

$200 Blackwell’s Wine and Spirits

Mocel Mezcal Artesanal Ensamble

Herbaceous, zesty and complex, this ensemble mezcal (made with a blend of agave varieties) opens with lively, mouthwatering lime peel, lemongrass and pine, winding into rosemary and tarragon midpalate. The long exhale finishes with cubeb pepper and pink peppercorn snap. Limited edition of 582 bottles. 95 Points — K.N.

$232 Tipxy

Cazcanes Destilado de Agave Nuestras Raices Still Strength Blanco

Note: this is not certified as a tequila nor mezcal, it’s a destilado de agave (agave distillate). Nomenclature be damned – this is an exquisite spirit. It’s downright kaleidoscopic, by turns citrusy, vegetal, lightly spiced, ever-changing from one sip to the next. But if it must be pinned down: expect a zesty aroma and a lively, complex, bold flavor. Tons of bell pepper and jalapeno, lime, and surprising hint of cacao give way to an extraordinarily long finish showing crumbled sage, slivers of lime peel, and ginger root, extinguished by a final cayenne flicker. This is one to sip and share. 2025 Special Edition. Nuestras Raices means “our roots.” 100 Points — K.N.
